detail.question: What does Mill claim about the abilities of women who have ruled as queens or regents?
detail.answer: Mill argues that women who have held power have shown real ability. He says that few queens have reigned compared with kings, but "a far larger proportion" of them "have shown talents for rule", often in difficult periods. They were noted for firmness and vigour as well as intelligence, which runs against the conventional picture of women's character. Adding regents and viceroys makes the list of eminent women rulers very long (John Stuart Mill, The Subjection of Women, Chapter 3, paragraph 5 (edition-specific)). He holds that it is certain a woman can be a Queen Elizabeth, a Deborah or a Joan of Arc, because this is fact, not inference (John Stuart Mill, The Subjection of Women, Chapter 3, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)). He answers the jibe that men govern under queens by saying that most great queens were great by their own talents for government and kept the supreme direction of affairs in their own hands. If they chose good advisers, that shows their judgment (John Stuart Mill, The Subjection of Women, Chapter 3, paragraph 6 (edition-specific)). He also cites women who governed for kings. Two princesses ruled in a manner hardly equalled by their contemporaries, and Charles V's two governors of the Netherlands ruled very successfully, one of them, Margaret of Austria, being among the ablest politicians of her age (John Stuart Mill, The Subjection of Women, Chapter 3, paragraph 6 (edition-specific)). In a footnote, he says that from his official knowledge of Hindoo governments, in three cases out of four a well-governed principality is under a woman's rule. These women act as legal regents during an heir's minority and had no public experience or political books, so he calls their example of natural capacity for government "very striking" (John Stuart Mill, The Subjection of Women, Note footnote_2_1 to Chapter 3, paragraph 5 (edition-specific)). He concludes that wherever women's capacities for government have been tried, they have been found adequate in proportion. He attributes this to princesses having been allowed the same range of interests and freedom as men (John Stuart Mill, The Subjection of Women, Chapter 3, paragraph 7 (edition-specific)).

In the clearest case, Kant says an understanding that does not reflect on the sources of its own cognition cannot determine "the bounds that limit its employment" or know what lies within or outside "its own sphere." The critique likewise forbids creating "a new field of objects" beyond phenomena and straying into "intelligible worlds" (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Analytic, Appendix, paragraph 28 (edition-specific)). The passages do not single out one image as "the" metaphor. The territory/boundary imagery, with the empty space beyond the border, is the most consistent.

detail.answer:
For Kant, the understanding is the source of all combining (conjunction) of the manifold, that is, the diverse content of our representations. The senses can supply the manifold in intuition, but they never supply its conjunction. Conjunction is a spontaneous act of the faculty of representation, and that faculty, distinguished from sensibility, is called understanding (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Analytic, Book I, Chapter 2, §11, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). Kant calls this act synthesis. By it we cannot represent anything as conjoined in the object without having conjoined it ourselves (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Analytic, Book I, Chapter 2, §11, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). Synthesis means joining different representations and comprehending their diversity in one cognition. Kant calls it the first requisite for producing cognition (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Analytic, Book I, Chapter 1, §6, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)).

The understanding also supplies the unity of this combining. The same function that unifies representations in a judgement also unifies the synthesis of the manifold in intuition, and this unity is the pure conception of the understanding (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Analytic, Book I, Chapter 1, §6, paragraph 6 (edition-specific)). In the sequence Kant lays out, the diversity of pure intuition is given first. The imagination synthesizes it second, but this alone gives no cognition. The understanding gives the conceptions that unify this synthesis third (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Analytic, Book I, Chapter 1, §6, paragraph 5 (edition-specific)). Another passage links the synthesis of representations to the imagination and its synthetical unity to the unity of apperception (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Analytic, Book II, Chapter 2, Section II, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)). Every union of representations requires unity of consciousness in their synthesis, and this unity makes it possible for representations to relate to an object (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Analytic, Book I, Chapter 2, §13, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)). Kant describes the synthetical unity of apperception as the highest point to which every operation of the understanding must be connected, and says this faculty is the understanding itself (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Analytic, Book I, Chapter 2, §12, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)).

Finally, analysis presupposes synthesis. Where the understanding has not previously conjoined, it cannot dissect, because what is analysed must first have been given as conjoined by it (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Analytic, Book I, Chapter 2, §11, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)).

detail.question: What criticism does Hume make of philosophers who claim that all power belongs directly to God?
detail.answer: Hume says these philosophers defeat their own purpose. They strip nature and all created beings of every power so that everything depends more obviously and immediately on God (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section VII, Part I, §56, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). That view holds that God is "the immediate and sole cause of every event" in nature, and that what we call causes are only "occasions" (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section VII, Part I, §55, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). Hume replies that by this theory they "diminish, instead of magnifying" the grandeur of the divine attributes they want to celebrate. He argues that it shows more power in the Deity to delegate some power to inferior creatures than to produce everything by his own immediate volition. He also argues that it shows more wisdom to design the world at the start with such foresight that it serves all the purposes of providence by its own operation, than to have the Creator adjust its parts at every moment (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section VII, Part I, §56, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
Wollstonecraft says children should not be taught to make allowances for their parents' faults. Her reason is that every such allowance weakens the force of reason in their minds and makes them more indulgent to their own faults (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 11, paragraph 18 (edition-specific)). She distinguishes this from adult virtue. Being severe with oneself and forbearing to others is, in her words, one of the "most sublime virtues of maturity", whereas children "should only be taught the simple virtues" (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 11, paragraph 18 (edition-specific)). If they learn too early to make allowance for human passions and manners, they "wear off the fine edge of the criterion" by which they should regulate their own conduct, and they become unjust in proportion as they grow indulgent (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 11, paragraph 18 (edition-specific)). She also concludes that teaching virtue on any solid principle amounts to teaching children to despise their parents, and she finds that a difficulty for the instructor (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 11, paragraph 18 (edition-specific)).

Related passages give context. She calls the duty of obeying a parent merely because he is a parent "absurd", since it shackles the mind and prepares it for slavish submission to any power but reason (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 11, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)). She gives an example of a girl scolded because her mother's hair was ill-dressed, and asks what respect a girl could acquire for such a parent without doing violence to reason (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Note block 13 to Chapter 11, paragraph 17 (edition-specific)). She says parents who set a good example and let it work seldom fail to produce filial respect (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 11, paragraph 13 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer: Hobbes lists four abuses of speech, and the first is the one that makes people deceive themselves. It happens when men "register their thoughts wrong" because the meaning of their words is inconstant (unstable). As a result they record as their conceptions something they never conceived, and so deceive themselves (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part I, Chapter 4, Abuses Of Speech, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)). By contrast, he says the metaphorical use of words, in a sense other than the one they were ordained for, deceives others (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part I, Chapter 4, Abuses Of Speech, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer: Wollstonecraft attacks these arguments in several ways. (1) She says the reasoning from natural weakness is illogical. Even if woman is naturally weaker, she asks why it would follow that she should labour to become weaker than nature intended. She calls such arguments an insult to common sense that savour of passion. She also compares the "divine right of husbands" to the divine right of kings, and says it may be contested (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 3, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)). (2) She rejects feigned weakness as a way to win a husband's affection. A wife who has kept her natural strength should not pretend to a sickly delicacy. Weakness may excite tenderness and gratify man's arrogant pride, but it does not satisfy a mind that deserves respect, and fondness is a poor substitute for friendship (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 2, paragraph 42 (edition-specific)). (3) She reports and opposes the inference, drawn by the writer she is criticizing, that women should be weak and passive because they have less bodily strength. That writer concludes that woman was formed to please and be subject to man, and that being agreeable to her master is the grand end of her existence (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 5, §1, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)). (4) She argues that duty must rest on reason. Women cannot be bound by a duty they do not comprehend, and without understanding, no authority can make them perform it virtuously. Enforced subordination produces "convenient slaves" and degrades both master and dependent (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Dedication, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)). (5) She claims that artificial weakness has bad effects. It produces a propensity to tyrannize and breeds cunning. She says that if these prejudices are not fostered, women will fall into a subordinate yet respectable station (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Introduction, paragraph 15 (edition-specific)). This is a qualified point, since she does not deny a subordinate station outright. (6) She argues that weakness defeats the very duties it is supposed to serve. Family management and the education of children require strength of body and mind. She says reason is absolutely necessary for a woman to perform any duty properly, and that sensibility is not reason (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 4, paragraph 45 (edition-specific)). Fortitude presupposes strength of mind, which indolent acquiescence, asking advice instead of using one's own judgment, and obeying through fear cannot give. Her conclusion is to make women rational creatures and free citizens, and they will quickly become good wives and mothers, provided men do not neglect their own duties as husbands and fathers (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 12, paragraph 82 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
Wollstonecraft's test is whether a reason can be given. She defines a prejudice as a "fond obstinate persuasion, for which we can give no reason." As soon as a reason can be given for an opinion, it stops being a prejudice, even if it turns out to be an error in judgment (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 5, §5, paragraph 28 (edition-specific)).

She adds a historical point. Opinions of every kind were probably founded on some reason at first. They become prejudices when they are "indolently adopted" only because age has made them look venerable, and the original reason has ceased to be a reason or can no longer be traced (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 5, §5, paragraph 28 (edition-specific)).

She also points to signs of a prejudice. One is that men often use their reason to justify prejudices they have absorbed, they cannot trace how, instead of rooting them out (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 1, paragraph 7 (edition-specific)). Another is taking opinions on credit and submitting to authority, which leaves people unable to analyze opinions (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 2, paragraph 21 (edition-specific)). A third is that people who hold opinions without fully understanding them maintain them obstinately, like "echoes" of a relation or friend. She says she has often traced this and ventures to affirm that a person of moderate abilities who asserts an opinion with heat is very often voicing a prejudice (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 5, §5, paragraph 27 (edition-specific)). She suggests heat may also reveal wavering, since people tend to assert opinions most hotly when they begin to doubt them (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 5, §5, paragraph 29 (edition-specific)).

By contrast, those who are convinced they have a right to what they insist on do not fear reason or the sifting of subjects (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 10, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)). This is the nearest the passages come to describing a reasoned position. They do not give a full list of criteria beyond this.

detail.answer:
Smith says the difference lies in how concentrated or spread out the dependence is. When great landowners spend their rents on tenants and retainers, each one maintains all of his own tenants and retainers entirely (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book III, Chapter 4, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)). Tenants at will and retainers were alike dependent on the proprietor: their subsistence came from his bounty, and its continuance depended on his good pleasure (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book III, Chapter 4, paragraph 6 (edition-specific)).

When the same landowners spend on tradesmen and artificers, taken together they may maintain as many people as before, or even more, because of the waste that attends rustic hospitality. Taken singly, however, each landowner contributes only a very small share to the maintenance of any individual tradesman (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book III, Chapter 4, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)). A tradesman lives from the custom of a hundred or a thousand customers. He is therefore somewhat obliged to them all but not absolutely dependent on any one (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book III, Chapter 4, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)).

Smith also describes the shift in spending that underlies this contrast. Once landowners could exchange their whole surplus for goods to consume themselves, they no longer shared it with tenants or retainers, and they gave up the authority that sharing had given them (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book III, Chapter 4, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)).

detail.question: Why does Kant argue that scepticism provides definitive answers to the problems of reason?
detail.premise: Kant holds that scepticism provides solutions to the problems of reason.

expected.locator: Doctrine of Method, Chapter 1, Section II, paragraph 37 (edition-specific)

detail.answer:
Kant does not argue this. The passages say the opposite: scepticism does not give definitive answers to the problems of reason. He says the sceptical procedure "does not present any solution of the problems of reason". Its value is as an exercise that awakens reason's circumspection (carefulness) and points to how reason can establish its legitimate claims (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Doctrine of Method, Chapter 1, Section II, paragraph 37 (edition-specific)).

He gives several reasons for this.

1. Scepticism is aimed at the dogmatist, who builds a system without examining its foundations, and it can show the futility of that project. In itself, though, it gives no certain information about the bounds of our knowledge. It cannot settle the dispute over the rights and powers of human reason, or tell us whether reason can hope for better success in future (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Doctrine of Method, Chapter 1, Section II, paragraph 31 (edition-specific)).

2. Kant rejects a sceptical stance of neutrality in speculative disputes. Doubts can lead reason to moderate its confidence and listen to criticism, but we should not stop there. He will not treat the conviction of our ignorance as the settlement of reason's disputes with itself. Scepticism is only a means of awakening reason from its "dogmatic dreams" and prompting a more careful investigation of its own powers (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Doctrine of Method, Chapter 1, Section II, paragraph 24 (edition-specific)).

3. He criticizes the sceptical thinker he discusses (the passage does not name him) for declaring the understanding limited without showing what its limits are. That thinker created general mistrust without giving determinate knowledge of the bounds of our ignorance. His declarations were therefore themselves doubted, because they rested on contingent facts rather than principles (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Doctrine of Method, Chapter 1, Section II, paragraph 34 (edition-specific)).

4. Of the antinomy discussion, Kant says the transcendental dialectic "does not favour scepticism". It does, however, demonstrate the advantages of the sceptical method. The result was not a positive dogmatic addition to metaphysics, but it corrected our judgements (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Book II, Chapter 2, Section VII, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)).

So in these passages scepticism is a useful preparatory discipline, and the premise of the question is mistaken. The definite marking-out of limits comes from a systematic critical investigation of the understanding and reason, not from scepticism itself.

detail.question: How does Hume explain the occurrence of unexpected outcomes in the human body?
detail.answer: Hume explains unexpected outcomes in the body as the result of hidden causes, not as a breakdown in the laws of nature. When usual symptoms of health or sickness disappoint expectation, or medicines do not work with their usual powers, the philosopher and physician are not surprised. They do not deny the necessity and uniformity of the principles governing the animal economy (the workings of the body). They take the body to be a very complicated machine with many secret powers that lie beyond our comprehension, so it often appears uncertain in its operations. The irregular events we see on the outside therefore do not prove that the laws of nature fail in its internal workings (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section VIII, Part I, §67, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)). Hume gives a similar account of causes in general. Some causes, such as rhubarb as a purge or opium as a soporific, have not always worked for everyone. When a cause fails to produce its usual effect, philosophers do not blame irregularity in nature. They suppose that some secret causes in the particular structure of parts prevented the operation (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section VI, §47, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). He also says that causes are not all joined to their usual effects with the same uniformity (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section VIII, Part I, §67, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). The passages do not go into further detail about the body's hidden causes. They treat them as unknown to us.

detail.answer:
Locke says power, considered in relation to change, is two-fold: the ability to make a change and the ability to receive one. He calls the first ACTIVE power and the second PASSIVE power (John Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1 / MDCXC, Based on the 2nd Edition, Books 1 and 2, Volume 1, Book II, Chapter 21, §2, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)). He treats active power as the more proper sense of the word "power". Whenever we observe a change, the mind must infer a power somewhere able to make it, as well as a possibility in the thing itself to receive it. He adds that sensible things furnish many instances of passive power, because their qualities are in continual flux (John Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1 / MDCXC, Based on the 2nd Edition, Books 1 and 2, Volume 1, Book II, Chapter 21, §4, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)).

Locke also holds that bodies give us only an obscure idea of active power. A body at rest shows no active power to move. A body set in motion, such as a ball struck by a billiard-stick, is rather passive, because its motion is "rather a passion than an action" in it. When one ball strikes another, it only transfers motion it received and does not produce any. (John Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1 / MDCXC, Based on the 2nd Edition, Books 1 and 2, Volume 1, Book II, Chapter 21, §4, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)). The clearer idea of beginning motion comes from reflection on ourselves. By willing it, we find by experience that we can move parts of our bodies that were at rest. Bodies give us no idea in themselves of the power to begin any action, whether motion or thought (John Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1 / MDCXC, Based on the 2nd Edition, Books 1 and 2, Volume 1, Book II, Chapter 21, §4, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)). Locke says only that "it seems to me" this is so, and he allows that someone who finds a clear idea of power in the impulse of bodies serves his purpose equally well.

Locke also raises, without settling, whether matter is wholly without active power, whether God is above all passive power, and whether created spirits alone have both. He says these questions "may be worth consideration" and that he will not now pursue them. He suggests we look to God and spirits for the clearest idea of active power (John Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1 / MDCXC, Based on the 2nd Edition, Books 1 and 2, Volume 1, Book II, Chapter 21, §2, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)).

detail.question: Why does Mill claim that people always think only of their own pain when they feel their sense of justice has been violated?
detail.premise: Mill claims that people always think only of their own pain when they feel their sense of justice has been violated.
detail.answer:
Mill does not claim this. The passages show him rejecting the idea that people always think only of their own pain when their sense of justice is outraged. He is answering an objection to his doctrine, namely that when we feel our sentiment of justice outraged we are thinking only of the individual case, not of society or any collective interest. He says this is no objection (John Stuart Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 5, paragraph 22 (edition-specific)). He concedes that it is common, though 'the reverse of commendable', to feel resentment merely because we have suffered pain (John Stuart Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 5, paragraph 22 (edition-specific)). But he says a person whose resentment is a real moral feeling first considers whether the act is blameable. Such a person, even without saying so, feels he is asserting a rule that benefits others as well as himself. If someone regards the act solely as it affects him individually, Mill says he is not consciously just (John Stuart Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 5, paragraph 22 (edition-specific)).

The wider account supports this. Mill treats the desire to punish as a natural feeling of retaliation, made applicable by intellect and sympathy to hurts that wound us through, or in common with, society. In itself he says this has nothing moral in it. It becomes moral when it is subordinated to the social sympathies, so that it acts only in directions conformable to the general good (John Stuart Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 5, paragraph 21 (edition-specific)). The raw natural feeling, by contrast, tends to make us resent indiscriminately whatever is disagreeable to us (John Stuart Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 5, paragraph 21 (edition-specific)). So the passages treat self-focused resentment as a common, non-moral form of the feeling, and not as the universal or defining one.

top_retrieved.locator: Transcendental Dialectic, Book II, Chapter 1, paragraph 42 (edition-specific)

detail.answer:
Kant holds that we really do possess a priori synthetic cognitions. He takes their existence to be proved by the principles of the understanding, which anticipate experience (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Doctrine of Method, Chapter 1, Section II, paragraph 30 (edition-specific)). A skeptic who cannot comprehend how these principles are possible may doubt that they are a priori, but cannot declare them impossible or call the steps reason has taken under their guidance null. Kant also grants that doubt about dogmatic philosophy, which proceeds without criticism, is well grounded. Even so, reason is not denied the ability to build a sound philosophy once a thorough critical investigation has prepared the way (same passage).

On why such knowledge is puzzling, Kant uses the proposition "Everything that happens has a cause." The concept of a cause is not contained in the concept of "that which happens." Experience cannot supply the link, because the principle connects the two with universality and necessity, which experience cannot give (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Introduction, Section IV, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)). He adds that the whole aim of our speculative a priori knowledge depends on such synthetic, augmentative propositions. Analytic judgements matter only for the clarity of concepts they provide, and synthesis alone is a real acquisition (same passage). Metaphysics, as an attempted science that human reason cannot do without, must contain synthetic a priori propositions, since it seeks to widen our a priori knowledge beyond the limits of experience (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Introduction, Section V, paragraph 6 (edition-specific)).

On reason's responsibility, Kant says the concepts and questions produced by pure reason lie not in the sphere of experience but in reason itself. Reason must therefore solve them and show them to be either valid or inadmissible. We have no right to decline this task by appealing to the nature of things or to the limits of human faculties, because reason is the sole creator of these ideas and is bound either to establish their validity or to expose their illusory nature (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Doctrine of Method, Chapter 1, Section II, paragraph 30 (edition-specific)).

detail.question: How does Hume evaluate the effectiveness of Cartesian universal doubt in achieving certainty?
detail.answer:
Hume judges Cartesian universal doubt to be ineffective as a route to certainty when taken in its full form, though he allows a moderate version some value.

He describes the Cartesian proposal as a doubt of all our former opinions and even of our faculties, to be remedied by a chain of reasoning from some original principle that cannot be deceitful (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section XII, Part I, §116, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)). He raises two objections. First, no such original principle has a prerogative over other self-evident and convincing principles. Second, even if there were one, we could not advance a step beyond it except by using the very faculties we were supposedly distrusting (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section XII, Part I, §116, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)). His conclusion is that, were such doubt ever attainable (he says plainly it is not), it would be entirely incurable, and no reasoning could bring us to assurance and conviction on any subject (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section XII, Part I, §116, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)).

Hume does grant that this scepticism, when more moderate, can be understood in a reasonable sense. It is a necessary preparation for philosophy because it preserves impartiality and weans the mind from prejudices absorbed from education or rash opinion (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section XII, Part I, §116, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)). He adds that starting from clear and self-evident principles, advancing cautiously, and reviewing conclusions will make progress slow and short. These are nonetheless the only methods by which we can hope to reach truth and a proper stability and certainty (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section XII, Part I, §116, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)).

The passages do not say more about Descartes beyond this section, so my account is limited to these points.

detail.answer:
Hobbes says that "Just" and "Unjust" mean one thing when applied to people and another when applied to actions. Applied to men, they signify conformity or inconformity of manners (one's manner of life) to reason. Applied to actions, they signify conformity or inconformity to reason of particular actions (Hobbes, Leviathan, Part I, Chapter 15, Justice Of Men, And Justice Of Actions What, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)).

A just man is one who takes all the care he can that his actions be just, and an unjust man is one who neglects this. Such men are more often called "Righteous" and "Unrighteous", though the meaning is the same. A righteous man does not lose that title through one or a few unjust actions that come from sudden passion or mistakes. An unrighteous man does not lose his character through actions he does or avoids out of fear, because his will is shaped by apparent benefit rather than by justice (Hobbes, Leviathan, Part I, Chapter 15, Justice Of Men, And Justice Of Actions What, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)). The justice of manners is what is meant when justice is called a virtue and injustice a vice (Hobbes, Leviathan, Part I, Chapter 15, Justice Of Men, And Justice Of Actions What, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)).

He adds a second contrast. The injustice of manners is a disposition or aptitude to do injury. It is injustice before it proceeds to act, and it does not presuppose any individual person injured. The injustice of an action, that is, injury, presupposes an individual injured person, namely the one to whom the covenant was made (Hobbes, Leviathan, Part I, Chapter 15, Justice Of Manners, And Justice Of Actions, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)). This connects to his definition of injustice of action as the not performance of covenant: once a covenant is made, breaking it is unjust (Hobbes, Leviathan, Part I, Chapter 15, Justice And Injustice What, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
Burke urges his countrymen to hold up the British Constitution as an example for the French, rather than borrow French models to improve their own. He calls the Constitution "an invaluable treasure" (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 417 (edition-specific)).

He credits Britain's happy situation to the whole Constitution, not to any single part. It owes as much to what was left standing through past reviews and reforms as to what was altered or added (same passage). On this view, patriotic energy is best spent guarding what the British already possess from violation. Burke does not rule out alteration, but says that even when he changed something, it should be "to preserve." Any remedy should be prompted by a great grievance and follow the example of the ancestors, with repairs made as nearly as possible "in the style of the building" (same passage). He asks his countrymen to imitate their forefathers' caution, to add if they please but preserve what was left, and to be content to admire, rather than follow, "the aëronauts of France" in their "desperate flights" (same passage).

Burke also says the doctrine behind the French spirit of change is now publicly taught, which is why he wants attention called back to the true principles of Britain's own domestic laws. He wants the British to keep cherishing them and not be imposed upon by "counterfeit wares" of an "improved liberty" styled after Paris fashion (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 46 (edition-specific)). He describes the new French Constitution as "the very reverse of ours in its principle" and is astonished anyone would offer it as an example for Great Britain (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 326 (edition-specific)).

Burke's view of France's earlier government is not wholly negative. He thinks it was not so oppressive, corrupt, or negligent as to be unfit for all reformation, and that it deserved to have its faults corrected and its capacities "improved into a British Constitution" (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 234 (edition-specific)).

detail.question: How does Mill distinguish between types of government interference in trade?
detail.answer:
Mill separates interferences with trade mainly by whether they raise a question of individual liberty, and the passages support the following account.

1. Interferences that are not questions of liberty. Mill says trade is a social act, so a seller's conduct comes in principle within society's jurisdiction (John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)). Restrictions on trade are restraints, and every restraint as such is an evil. But they affect only the part of conduct that society is competent to restrain. They are wrong solely because they do not produce the results they aim at (John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)). This is the Free Trade doctrine, which rests on grounds different from, though equally solid with, the principle of individual liberty. Questions such as preventing fraud by adulteration, sanitary precautions, and protecting workers in dangerous occupations also do not essentially involve liberty. Leaving people alone is better, other things equal, but they may legitimately be controlled for these ends (John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)).

2. Interferences that are questions of liberty. Mill's examples are the Maine Law, the prohibition of importing opium into China, and the restriction of the sale of poisons. These are cases where the interference aims to make a commodity impossible or difficult to obtain (John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)). He says these are objectionable not as infringements on the liberty of the producer or seller, but on that of the buyer (John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)).

3. A further, separate category. Mill sets aside cases where the question is not about restraining individuals but about the government helping them, that is, whether it should do something for their benefit instead of leaving it to individuals or voluntary combination (John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 16 (edition-specific)). Objections to interference that does not infringe liberty are said to be of three kinds (John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 17 (edition-specific)). The passages give only two of them. The first is that individuals are likely to do the thing better than the government, which Mill says condemns old interferences with ordinary industry (John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 18 (edition-specific)). The third, which he calls the most cogent, is the great evil of adding unnecessarily to government power (John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 20 (edition-specific)). The second kind is not in the supplied passages, so I cannot report it.

detail.answer: Kant claims that using general logic as an organon (an instrument for producing knowledge) turns it into a "logic of illusion," which he calls dialectic. General logic teaches nothing about the content of our cognitions. It gives only the formal conditions of their accord with the understanding, and these are indifferent to objects. Any attempt to use it to extend and enlarge our knowledge therefore "must end in mere prating," so that anyone can maintain or oppose any assertion with some appearance of truth (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Logic, Introduction, Section III, paragraph 6 (edition-specific)). He adds that the mere form of a cognition cannot supply material (objective) truth, so logic alone cannot decide anything about objects without independently obtained information. Because of the charm of this art, which gives our cognitions the form of understanding even where content is lacking, general logic, which is merely a canon of judgement, has been used as an organon for the actual production, or rather the semblance of production, of objective assertions. Kant calls this a gross misapplication, and says that general logic in this assumed character of organon is called dialectic (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Logic, Introduction, Section III, paragraph 5 (edition-specific)).

He says its one certain effect is "producing an oligarchy in every one of the republics." He holds that a paper circulation not backed by real money, forced in place of the kingdom's coin and made the substance of its revenue and the medium of commerce, "must put the whole of what power, authority, and influence is left" into the hands of those who manage the circulation (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 331 (edition-specific)).

The closest idea to equality in the passages is a different one. Burke says the Assembly made the paper currency compulsory in all payments to "put every individual on the same bottom" and bind the nation in one guilty interest. He means this as a way to force everyone into sharing in the pillage of Church property and to secure the Assembly's own power. He does not mean it as an equal distribution of power (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 220 (edition-specific)). He also calls the compulsory paper currency an outrage upon "credit, property, and liberty" (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 221 (edition-specific)).

So the question's premise is not supported by the passages. They give no argument from Burke that the scheme spreads power equally among citizens.

detail.question: According to Mill, should society always punish individuals for personal failings such as imprudence or lack of dignity?
detail.premise: Mill believes society should punish individuals for personal failings even when these do not harm others.
detail.answer:
No. Mill holds that purely self-regarding faults such as imprudence or lack of personal dignity should not be punished, though they may properly cost a person other people's good opinion. He separates "the loss of consideration which a person may rightly incur by defect of prudence or of personal dignity" from the "reprobation" (strong condemnation) due for an offence against others' rights (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 4, paragraph 7 (edition-specific)). For self-regarding faults, we may express distaste and stand aloof, but we should not feel called on to make the person's life uncomfortable. Because he already bears the penalty of his own error, Mill says we should try to alleviate it rather than add to it. At worst we are justified in leaving him to himself (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 4, paragraph 7 (edition-specific)). Punishment is for those who infringe rules necessary to protect others, because then the harm falls on others and society, as protector of its members, must retaliate (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 4, paragraph 7 (edition-specific)).

Mill adds that the line is drawn at harm to others or breach of duty, not at the underlying vice. A man whose intemperance or extravagance leaves him unable to pay debts or support his family is blamed and might be justly punished, but for the breach of duty, not the extravagance (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 4, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)). Likewise, "No person ought to be punished simply for being drunk," though a soldier or policeman should be punished for being drunk on duty. Where there is definite damage or definite risk of damage to an individual or the public, the case moves from liberty to morality or law (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 4, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)). Drunkenness and idleness are not ordinarily fit subjects for legal punishment, though he allows exceptions. One is a person already convicted of violence while drunk. Another is someone who fails in legal duties to others, such as supporting his children (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 6 (edition-specific)).

Mill considers the objection that society should protect mature persons who are unfit for self-government, and should repress vices like gambling or idleness with law or social penalties (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 4, paragraph 9 (edition-specific)). He answers that the merely contingent or "constructive" injury such conduct does to society is an inconvenience society can afford to bear "for the sake of the greater good of human freedom" (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 4, paragraph 11 (edition-specific)). Society, he argues, has had the whole period of childhood to train people to rational conduct, and it has education, the authority of received opinion, and the natural penalties of others' distaste. It should not claim the further power to command and enforce obedience in personal concerns (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 4, paragraph 11 (edition-specific)). He also argues that coercion tends to frustrate better means of influencing conduct and provokes rebellion in independent characters (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 4, paragraph 11 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
Smith describes two linked changes: a shift in the relative value of the two metals, and a fall in the real value of both.

Relative value: before the American discoveries, an ounce of fine gold was worth about 10 to 12 ounces of fine silver in Europe's mines. About the middle of the last century (the 1700s), it was worth about 14 to 15 ounces. Gold therefore rose in nominal value, meaning the quantity of silver given for it (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book I, Chapter 11, Part III, paragraph 91 (edition-specific)).

Real value: in that passage, both metals sank in real value, meaning the quantity of labour they could purchase. Silver sank more than gold. Smith says the American silver mines seem to have been proportionally even more fertile than the gold ones (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book I, Chapter 11, Part III, paragraph 91 (edition-specific)).

Cause and timing: he says the discovery of the mines of America diminished the value of gold and silver in Europe (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book I, Chapter 5, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)). He says the abundant American mines seem to have been the sole cause of silver's fall in value against corn. Supply rose faster than demand, even though Europe was advancing in industry (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book I, Chapter 11, Part III, paragraph 50 (edition-specific)). Smith adds that the discovery did not seem to affect English prices much until after 1570 (same passage). He places the completion of silver's fall relative to corn around 1630–1640, and says its value seems never to have sunk lower than at that time (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book I, Chapter 11, Part III, paragraph 53 (edition-specific)).

Continuing decline: Smith is tentative about whether the fall continued. He says it is commonly supposed, though he thinks without certain proof, that the diminution is still going on gradually (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book I, Chapter 5, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)). Elsewhere he says it is supposed, perhaps without much foundation, that the metals have been steadily sinking in value because of continual imports from the Spanish West Indies (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book IV, Chapter 1, paragraph 14 (edition-specific)). In the same passage, he says the earlier fall in silver relative to corn seems to have reversed somewhat in the eighteenth century (Book I, Chapter 11, Part III, paragraph 53, above).

Effect on a country: because the degradation affects most of the commercial world about equally, Smith says it matters little to any one country. Money prices rise, but people are neither really richer nor really poorer. A service of plate becomes really cheaper, while other things keep the same real value (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book IV, Chapter 5, paragraph 16 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
Wollstonecraft's fullest account is in Chapter 1. She says that in the "infancy of society," when men were just emerging from barbarism, chiefs and priests had "unbounded sway" because they touched the most powerful springs of savage conduct, hope and fear (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 1, paragraph 29 (edition-specific)). She holds that an aristocracy is naturally the first form of government. Then, as clashing interests lost their equipoise (balance), a monarchy and hierarchy "break out of the confusion of ambitious struggles," and feudal tenures secure the foundation of both (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 1, paragraph 29 (edition-specific)). She presents this as "the origin of monarchial and priestly power, and the dawn of civilization" (same passage). Her wording is hedged: "must have had" and "appears to be."

She then describes how these powers changed. Wars, both foreign and internal, gave the people some power in the tumult, so rulers had to gloss over their oppression with a show of right. As wars, agriculture, commerce and literature expanded the mind, despots had to replace open force with "covert corruption." Luxury and superstition, which she calls the "dregs of ambition," spread this corruption most quickly (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 1, paragraph 29 (edition-specific)).

The passages give no more detail on early priestly power beyond this account. Other passages criticize the later effects of hereditary honours, riches and monarchy, but they do not describe early development (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 1, paragraph 11 (edition-specific)).

detail.question: What does Locke argue about the relationship between conquest and the establishment of government?
detail.answer:
Locke argues that conquest is not a source of government. Governments originally arise only from the consent of the people, but the noise of war has led many to mistake "the force of arms for the consent of the people" and to count conquest among the origins of government (Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 16, §175, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). He compares conquest to demolishing a house, which is not building a new one. Conquest often makes way for a new commonwealth by destroying the old one, but without the people's consent it can never erect a new one (Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 16, §175, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)).

He also limits what conquest can give a conqueror, even in a just war:
- He gets no power over those who fought alongside him; they remain freemen (Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 16, §177, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)). He applies this to the Norman conquest of England: even if William had a right to make war, his dominion could reach only the Saxons and Britons, not the Normans who helped him (Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 16, §177, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)).
- A conqueror in a just war has no right of dominion over those who joined him, over those of the subdued country who did not oppose him, or over the posterity of even those who did. They are free, and if their former government is dissolved, they may erect another for themselves (Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 16, §185, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)).
- In a just war, the conqueror's power over the conquered is "perfectly despotical", meaning absolute over the lives of those who forfeited them by making war. It gives him no right and title to their possessions (Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 16, §180, paragraph 7 (edition-specific)). Locke admits this may seem strange, since it runs contrary to the practice of the world, but he says the practice of the powerful is seldom the rule of right (Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 16, §180, paragraph 7 (edition-specific)).
- Harm suffered in the state of nature cannot let a conqueror dispossess the vanquished's posterity. Without right, conquest gives only the title that bare force gives the stronger over the weaker, so the strongest would have a right to whatever he seizes (Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 16, §184, paragraph 11 (edition-specific)).
- Even if a conqueror had a right to estates, absolute power would not follow. The descendants are freemen, and whatever he grants them they hold as property, which cannot be taken without their own consent (Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 16, §193, paragraph 20 (edition-specific)).
- One who conquers in an unjust war has no title to the subjection and obedience of the conquered (Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 16, §176, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)).

His conclusion is that a conqueror's government, imposed by force on those against whom he had no right of war, or who did not join the war against him where he had that right, has no obligation upon them (Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 16, §187, paragraph 14 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
The passages support only part of this premise. In Chapter 4, Wollstonecraft says that when treating of education or manners, "minds of a superior class are not to be considered, they may be left to chance" (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 4, paragraph 61 (edition-specific)). Her reason is that it is "the multitude, with moderate abilities, who call for instruction, and catch the colour of the atmosphere they breathe" (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 4, paragraph 61 (edition-specific)). In other words, she does not argue that only superior minds need structured education. She argues nearly the opposite: instruction matters most for ordinary people, while superior minds can be left to chance. She adds that these ordinary men and women need a "ballast of understanding" (ballast being a steadying weight), or they will never become virtuous or free (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 4, paragraph 61 (edition-specific)).

A related point appears in Chapter 12. There she imagines a later school where young people "of superior abilities, or fortune" would study languages, science, history and politics (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 12, paragraph 46 (edition-specific)). This is a further stage of education for those young people, not a claim that only they need education. The passages given do not explain how she would structure the earlier schooling for everyone else, so that question is left unanswered here.

detail.question: According to Hume, what distinguishes belief from mere imagination or fiction?
detail.answer:
Hume says belief is not a different idea but a different feeling or manner of conception. The imagination can freely mix, compound and divide ideas, and can feign events with every circumstance of time and place. Yet we cannot simply believe whatever we imagine. We can join the head of a man to the body of a horse in thought, but we cannot believe such an animal ever existed (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section V, Part II, §39, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). Belief is also not marked by some special idea added to the conception. The mind could attach any such idea to a fiction at will, and then believe whatever it pleased (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section V, Part II, §39, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)).

Instead, the difference lies in a sentiment or feeling annexed to belief and not to fiction. This feeling does not depend on the will and cannot be commanded at pleasure. It arises from nature, from the mind's situation at the time. When an object is present to memory or senses, custom carries the imagination to conceive the object usually conjoined with it, and that conception carries a feeling unlike the loose reveries of the fancy (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section V, Part II, §39, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)). Hume's example is the billiard-ball. Conceiving the ball stopping on contact is no contradiction, but it feels very different from conceiving the communication of motion (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section V, Part II, §39, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)).

Hume admits that defining this sentiment may be very difficult, if not impossible. He offers a description: belief is a more vivid, lively, forcible, firm, steady conception of an object than the imagination alone can reach. It makes realities weigh more in thought and gives them a superior influence on the passions and imagination. He says belief consists not in the nature or order of ideas but in the manner of their conception and their feeling to the mind (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section V, Part II, §40, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). In philosophy we can go no further than saying belief is something felt by the mind that distinguishes the ideas of the judgement from the fictions of the imagination. It gives them more weight and makes them the governing principle of our actions. The remembered voice of an acquaintance, for instance, takes faster hold of the mind than the idea of an enchanted castle (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section V, Part II, §40, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)).

Hume summarizes this as a conception more intense and steady than what attends the mere fictions of the imagination, arising from a customary conjunction of the object with something present to memory or senses. He frames this as a supposition he is willing to allow (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section V, Part II, §40, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)). Belief in matters of fact is derived from a present object plus customary conjunction, and is the necessary result of the mind's circumstances (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section V, Part I, §38, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer: Kant says the test is a simple question he puts to himself: "Canst thou also will that thy maxim should be a universal law?" (Immanuel Kant, Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals, First Section, paragraph 18 (edition-specific)). A maxim is the principle one acts on. If the answer is no, the maxim must be rejected. The reason is not a disadvantage to himself or to others. It is that the maxim cannot enter as a principle into a possible universal legislation, and reason extorts from him immediate respect for such legislation (Immanuel Kant, Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals, First Section, paragraph 18 (edition-specific)). He adds that he does not yet see what this respect rests on, and he leaves that question to the philosopher. He does understand that acting from pure respect for the practical law is what constitutes duty, and that this is the condition of a will being good in itself (Immanuel Kant, Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals, First Section, paragraph 18 (edition-specific)). A later passage links this to the idea that a good will's maxims are capable of making themselves a universal law (Immanuel Kant, Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals, Second Section, paragraph 89 (edition-specific)). The passages do not say how one can be certain that the test was actually followed. One passage warns that we can never be completely sure our real motive was duty rather than a secret impulse of self-love (Immanuel Kant, Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals, Second Section, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
Smith says wages of labour differ more from place to place than the price of provisions does. Bread and butchers' meat cost the same or nearly the same through most of the united kingdom, and goods sold by retail are generally as cheap or cheaper in great towns than in remoter parts (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book I, Chapter 8, paragraph 29 (edition-specific)). Wages in a great town and its neighbourhood are often a fourth or fifth higher than a few miles away. His examples: eighteen pence a day in London and its neighbourhood, falling to fourteen or fifteen pence a few miles off; tenpence in Edinburgh, falling to eightpence a few miles off (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book I, Chapter 8, paragraph 29 (edition-specific)). He argues that such a gap, which is apparently not always enough to move a man from one parish to another, shows that man is the most difficult 'luggage' to transport (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book I, Chapter 8, paragraph 29 (edition-specific)).

Smith adds that wages and provisions do not simply move together. Variations in the price of labour do not always match those in provisions and are frequently opposite. Still, the price of provisions does influence the money price of labour, which is regulated by the demand for labour and the price of necessaries and conveniencies of life. So labour may be dear where provisions are cheap, but it would be even dearer if provisions were also dear, with demand unchanged (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book I, Chapter 8, paragraph 50 (edition-specific)).

On the cause of unequal wages between nearby places in England, Smith says it is 'probably' the law of settlements, which obstructs a poor man moving from one parish to another without a certificate. detail.answer:
Burke thinks the French ministers are trapped in a humiliating and perilous office for several connected reasons.

1. Their office has lost its dignity and glory. In other countries the office of minister of state is of the highest dignity, but in France Burke calls it "full of peril, and incapable of glory" (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 350 (edition-specific)).

2. They are open to attack but cannot answer it. Rivals, enabled by the Constitution, can attack them in their vital parts, while the ministers can reply only "in the degrading character of culprits". Burke also says they are the only people in France incapable of a share in the national councils (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 350 (edition-specific)).

3. Responsibility is a poor substitute for active service. Burke grants that responsibility prevents crimes and makes attempts against the laws dangerous. But he says it cannot produce zealous service, and that "the elevation of mind to be derived from fear will never make a nation glorious" (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 350 (edition-specific)).

4. They lack the confidence of both the king and the Assembly. Each side forced them on the other, so their relations are marked by mutual counteraction. The Assembly's committees carry out the noble functions of their office with no regard to the ministers' personal or official authority. Burke describes them as being "in a species of subordinate servitude in which no men before them were ever seen" (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 353 (edition-specific); paragraph 350 for the point about mutual counteraction).

5. They are contradicted in every part of their role. They must "execute, without power", be "responsible, without discretion", and "deliberate, without choice". Serving two sovereigns over neither of whom they have influence, they must sometimes betray one, sometimes the other, and always themselves (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 353 (edition-specific)).

6. They must watch the damage done by the Revolution. Burke says they stand on "an eminence of humiliation" and must see the evils the Revolution has produced. He adds that they felt the degraded situation of their country and their own utter incapacity to serve it (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 353 (edition-specific)). He is astonished they have not resigned already, and says he would not have stood in their situation for the universe (same passage).

Burke assumes, without claiming to know, that the ministers wished the Revolution well ("I take it for granted"). He says the same predicament will face their successors (same passage).

detail.answer:
Locke says that someone who seeks truth on his own thinking will find satisfaction in the pursuit itself, whatever he ends up discovering. In the Epistle to the Reader, he describes a person who has "raised himself above the alms-basket" and does not "live lazily on scraps of begged opinions" (that is, on opinions taken from others), but sets his own thoughts to work finding and following truth. Such a person "will (whatever he lights on) not miss the hunter's satisfaction." Every moment of the pursuit rewards his pains with some delight, and he can think his time well spent even if he cannot boast of any great acquisition (Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1, THE EPISTLE TO THE READER, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)). He grounds this in an analogy: the understanding, like the eye, judging only by its own sight, is pleased with what it discovers and regrets less what has escaped it, because that is unknown (same passage).

Two other passages support this view. Locke contrasts real knowledge with trust in others: in the sciences each person has only as much as he really knows and comprehends, while what he merely believes on trust is "shreds" that add little to his stock, like "borrowed wealth" that turns to leaves and dust (Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1, Book I, Chapter 4, §24, paragraph 28 (edition-specific)). He also says that there is pleasure in knowledge, which "nobody...so senseless" would deny (Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1, Book II, Chapter 21, §44, paragraph 45 (edition-specific)). However, he adds a qualification: this pleasure moves a person's desire only if he counts it as part of his own happiness. Someone who places his satisfaction in sensual pleasures can acknowledge the delight of knowledge without being moved to pursue it (same passage).

The passages do not say more about the satisfaction of independent inquiry than this.

detail.answer:
Smith says the way taxes are collected in France makes a large difference to how much of what the people pay actually reaches the crown. Of the eight main sources of French revenue, the taille, the capitation and the two vingtiemes are levied by an administration under the immediate inspection and direction of government. The gabelles, aides, traites, domaine and tobacco farm are, in most provinces, under farm, meaning they are let out to private collectors. It is "universally acknowledged" that the government-run taxes bring more into the prince's treasury in proportion to what they take from the people. The farmed taxes are administered in a much more wasteful and expensive way (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book V, Chapter 2, Part II, paragraph 205 (edition-specific)).

Smith's proposed reforms follow from this. He suggests making the gabelle, aides, traites, tobacco taxes, customs and excises uniform across the kingdom, so they could be levied at much less expense. He also suggests putting all of them under direct government administration. He adds that replacing the taille and capitation with more vingtiemes could preserve the crown's revenue and greatly reduce collection costs (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book V, Chapter 2, Part II, paragraph 206 (edition-specific)). The passage on the third reform breaks off mid-sentence, so I rely only on what it states.

Smith also notes that France's overall yield is poor. In 1765 and 1766 the treasury received under fifteen millions sterling, less than half of what might have been expected if people had contributed in proportion to their numbers as in Great Britain. Yet the French are generally acknowledged to be much more oppressed by taxes (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book V, Chapter 2, Part II, paragraph 207 (edition-specific)). Smith presents these accounts as "very imperfect." He does not here tie this shortfall to any single collection method.

The assessment methods for the taille also have weaknesses. Smith says the council can never match assessments to real ability to pay, because ignorance and misinformation mislead it. He adds that assessors are said to be swayed by friendship, party animosity and private resentment (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book V, Chapter 2, Part II, paragraph 86 (edition-specific)). By contrast, the capitation always produces the sum expected, because each generality is assessed a fixed sum that the intendant must find, with extra assessment to cover those who cannot pay (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book V, Chapter 2, Part II, paragraph 126 (edition-specific)). This ensures yield, but it is severe on contributors.

The passages do not give figures comparing the actual collection costs of the different taxes.

detail.question: Why does Locke argue that private property is never justified, even in the earliest societies?
detail.premise: Locke holds that private property is never justified, even in the earliest societies.
detail.answer:
The question's premise is mistaken: the passages show Locke arguing the opposite. He holds that private property is justified, even in the earliest societies, and that it arises from labour. The passages do not support the claim that he thinks property is never justified.

Locke starts from the view that God gave the earth to mankind in common (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 5, §25, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). He then sets out to show how men might come to have a property in parts of that common inheritance without any express compact of all the commoners (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 5, §25, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)).

His answer is labour. A man is master of himself and proprietor of his own person and its labour, which is the "great foundation of property" (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 5, §44, paragraph 23 (edition-specific)). Whoever mixes labour with something common removes it from the state of nature and begins a property in it, as with the deer, the fish, or the hare (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 5, §30, paragraph 6 (edition-specific)). In the beginning, labour gave a right of property wherever someone employed it on what was common (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 5, §45, paragraph 24 (edition-specific)). Locke says that without assuming Adam's private dominion, labour can give distinct titles to parcels for private use, with no room for doubt or quarrel (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 5, §39, paragraph 16 (edition-specific)).

Locke does attach limits to early property. A man may not let what he takes spoil. If fruits rotted or venison putrified before he could use them, he offended against the common law of nature and invaded his neighbour's share (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 5, §37, paragraph 14 (edition-specific)). Nature also set the measure of property by the extent of men's labour and the conveniencies of life, so that no one could injure another. Each person left room for others to have "as good, and as large a possession" (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 5, §36, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)).

Locke also says that in the first peopling of the world the law man was under favoured appropriating. God commanded him to subdue the earth, and the condition of human life "necessarily introduces private possessions" (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 5, §35, paragraph 11 (edition-specific)). Where land is common by compact, as in England, no one may enclose it without the consent of the other commoners (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 5, §35, paragraph 11 (edition-specific)). Later, communities settled boundaries and regulated property by laws and agreement (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 5, §45, paragraph 24 (edition-specific)).

detail.question: What does Mill say about the familiarity of the reasons supporting liberty of thought and expression?
detail.answer:
Mill says the reasons behind liberty of thought and expression are less familiar than one might expect. He grants that these liberties, "to some considerable amount," already form part of the political morality of countries with religious toleration and free institutions. Even so, he says the philosophical and practical grounds on which they rest are "perhaps not so familiar to the general mind, nor so thoroughly appreciated by many even of the leaders of opinion, as might have been expected" (John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 1, paragraph 16 (edition-specific)). His wording is tentative ("perhaps"). He adds that these grounds, when rightly understood, apply much more widely than to this one branch of the subject. He also acknowledges that the topic has been discussed for about three centuries, and he asks the indulgence of readers to whom nothing he says will be new (John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 1, paragraph 16 (edition-specific)).

A related point comes in Chapter 2. There he says one aspect of the question, the liberty of the press as a safeguard against corrupt or tyrannical government, has been "so often and so triumphantly enforced by preceding writers" that it need not be insisted on there (John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 2, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). detail.answer:
Locke presents himself as willing to give up his opinions when truth appears against them, and he says he actually changed his mind on liberty and the will.

- He says he seeks only truth, and that he would sooner renounce an opinion of his own than oppose another person's view when truth is against it (John Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1 / MDCXC, Based on the 2nd Edition, Books 1 and 2, Volume 1, THE EPISTLE TO THE READER, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)).
- In the Epistle he says that on closer inspection he found reason to alter his earlier thoughts about what finally determines the Will in voluntary actions, and that he acknowledges this freely (same Epistle passage).
- In Book II, Chapter 21, §74 he calls himself "a lover of truth, and not a worshipper of my own doctrines" and admits some change of opinion from the earlier edition. He claims neither infallibility nor a wish to hide his mistakes to protect his reputation (John Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1 / MDCXC, Based on the 2nd Edition, Books 1 and 2, Volume 1, Book II, Chapter 21, §74, paragraph 84 (edition-specific)). He accepts that readers may judge his former or his later notions right, or neither. He would also be grateful to anyone who could clear the subject of liberty of its remaining difficulties (same §74 passage).
- In §73 he says he feared a mistake in his treatment of liberty, and a friend suspected one. A stricter review led him to a slip he had made in putting "one seemingly indifferent word for another", and this gave him the view he submits in the second edition (John Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1 / MDCXC, Based on the 2nd Edition, Books 1 and 2, Volume 1, Book II, Chapter 21, §73, paragraph 83 (edition-specific)).
- His openness has limits. He says he has not gained any light from the published objections to his book and has found no reason from them to alter his sense of the questioned points (Epistle, paragraph 10).
- Earlier in the Essay, not specifically about liberty, he says he would not be sorry to be convinced that he has been too fond of his own notions (John Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1 / MDCXC, Based on the 2nd Edition, Books 1 and 2, Volume 1, Book I, Chapter 2, §28, paragraph 29 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
Kant describes reason's logical use as the faculty of conclusion, or "mediate judgement" (inference through a middle step). It works by subsuming (placing under) the condition of one possible judgement beneath the condition of a given judgement (Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Book I, Section II, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)).

The steps are as follows:
- The given judgement is the general rule, called the major. The subsumption of the condition of another possible judgement under the rule's condition is the minor. The actual judgement that asserts the rule in the subsumed case is the conclusion (Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Book I, Section II, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)).
- In his first-person account, the rule is thought by the understanding, the minor subsumes a cognition under the rule's condition by means of judgement, and the conclusion determines the cognition by the rule's predicate. Kant says this determination is made à priori by reason (Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Introduction, Section II, paragraph 11 (edition-specific)).
- The underlying logic is that the rule asserts something generally under a condition. When that condition is met in a particular case, what held generally must also hold in that case (Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Book I, Section II, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)).

Kant's example runs from "All compound is changeable" to "Bodies are compound" and then to "Bodies are changeable." He calls this reaching a cognition through a series of conditions (premisses) (Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Book I, Section II, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)).

Because the rule can itself be subjected to the same process, reason can seek the condition of the condition. Kant concludes that reason's peculiar principle is to find the unconditioned for the conditioned cognition of the understanding, which completes its unity (Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Introduction, Section II, paragraph 16 (edition-specific)). Such a series of syllogisms can be continued indefinitely (Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Book I, Section II, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)). Reason thereby tries to bring the variety of the understanding's cognitions under the fewest possible principles, producing the highest unity (Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Introduction, Section II, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)).

Kant also distinguishes two employments of reason. In the demonstrative (apodeictic) employment, the general is certain and given, so the particular is necessarily determined once it is subsumed under it. In the hypothetical employment, the general is only problematical, a mere idea. Particular cases are then tested, and if all that can be collected follow from the rule, its universality is inferred (Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Appendix, paragraph 6 (edition-specific)).
