detail.question: What does Kant say about the reality of the object associated with the idea of systematic unity?
detail.answer: Kant denies that the object tied to the idea of systematic unity is real absolutely or in itself. He says reason cannot think this unity without also thinking an object of the idea, one that no experience can present. That object is "a mere idea" and is not assumed to be a thing real in itself. It is only the "problematical foundation" (a hypothetical ground) of the connection the mind introduces among phenomena. We regard that connection "as if" it came from the supposed being, but all we aim at is a secure foundation for the systematic unity of experience (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Appendix, paragraph 46 (edition-specific)). The same point appears for the idea of a supreme intelligence. Its objective reality does not lie in any immediate relation to an object, and we cannot establish objective validity in that sense. The idea is a "heuristic", not an "ostensive", conception. It does not tell us how an object is constituted, but only how to investigate objects in experience (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Appendix, paragraph 37 (edition-specific)). Kant also names the error of treating the idea as a real object: we "hypostatize" the principle of systematic unity (treat it as a real thing) and give it an anthropomorphic determination. He says this reverses the proper procedure of reason and in effect loses the unity of nature (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Appendix, paragraph 54 (edition-specific)). There are qualifications. Systematic unity is certainly a logical principle. Asserting that objects themselves are determined to such unity would need a transcendental principle of reason (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Appendix, paragraph 9 (edition-specific)). Kant also says that, in relation to the criterion of empirical truth, we must suppose the idea of the systematic unity of nature to have objective validity and necessity (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Appendix, paragraph 13 (edition-specific)). Finally, he remarks that it is "very natural" to assume a legislative reason corresponding to the idea of unity. He presents this as a natural assumption, not as a proof of such a being's existence (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Appendix, paragraph 56 (edition-specific)). Taken together, the passages describe the idea's object as a regulative, heuristic posit, valid for guiding inquiry but not established as a real thing in itself.

detail.answer:
Hobbes says the word Church (Ecclesia) "signifieth" several different things in Scripture. He lists these senses:

1. A house. Sometimes, though not often, it means God's House, a Temple where Christians assemble for holy duties. Hobbes calls this a metaphor for the congregation assembled there, and says the word was later used for the building itself (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part III, Chapter 39, Church The Lords House, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)).

2. An assembly. When not taken for a house, Church means what Ecclesia meant in the Grecian Common-wealths: a congregation or assembly of citizens called forth to hear the Magistrate. If lawful authority called them, it was a lawful Church. If tumultuous and seditious clamor excited them, it was a confused Church (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part III, Chapter 39, Ecclesia Properly What, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)).

3. Several other senses. It can mean the men who have a right to be of the congregation though not actually assembled, that is, the whole multitude of Christian men however dispersed. It can mean a certain part of Christians, or the Elect only (the Church Triumphant, or Church To Come). It can also mean an assembled congregation of professors of Christianity, whether their profession is true or counterfeit (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part III, Chapter 39, Ecclesia Properly What, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)).

Hobbes adds that only in this last sense can the Church be taken as one Person, able to will, command, make laws or act. He then defines a Church as a company of men professing Christian Religion, united in the person of one Soveraign (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part III, Chapter 39, In What Sense The Church Is One Person Church Defined, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)).

So the sovereign must judge opinions as something necessary to peace, to prevent discord and civil war (same passage). Other passages fit this view. detail.question: Why does Hume claim that the opposite of any matter of fact is impossible to conceive without contradiction?
detail.premise: Hume claims that the opposite of any matter of fact is impossible to conceive without contradiction.
detail.answer:
Hume's reasoning rests on a contrast between matters of fact and demonstrable truths. In the *Enquiry*, he says the contrary of every matter of fact is still possible because it can never imply a contradiction, and the mind conceives it as easily and distinctly as the truth (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section IV, Part I, §21, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). His example is that "the sun will not rise to-morrow" is no less intelligible, and no more contradictory, than the claim that it will rise (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section IV, Part I, §21, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). He adds that if such a claim were demonstratively false, it would imply a contradiction and could never be distinctly conceived. Since it can be distinctly conceived, its falsehood cannot be demonstrated (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section IV, Part I, §21, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)).

He generalizes the point in Section XII. Enquiries about matter of fact and existence are "evidently incapable of demonstration". The non-existence of any being is as clear and distinct an idea as its existence. A proposition denying a being is false but no less conceivable and intelligible than one affirming it (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section XII, Part III, §132, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). The sciences are different: in them a false proposition is confused and unintelligible. His example is that the cube root of 64 equals half of 10, which can never be distinctly conceived. By contrast, that Caesar or the angel Gabriel never existed is a false proposition that is still perfectly conceivable and implies no contradiction (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section XII, Part III, §132, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)).

The billiard-ball example in Section V illustrates this. Hume says no matter of fact is believed so firmly that we cannot conceive the contrary. We can easily conceive a ball stopping on contact, and this conception implies no contradiction, though it feels different from the conception of the impulse communicating motion (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section V, Part II, §39, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)).

The passages themselves do not set out a fuller argument for why thought is so unrestricted. One related remark is that nothing is beyond the power of thought except what implies an absolute contradiction (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section II, §13, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)).

detail.question: What does Hume suggest about the origins of widely believed extraordinary stories?
detail.answer:
Hume suggests that widely believed extraordinary stories typically arise from ordinary human tendencies, not from real violations of nature. He points to several sources.

1. A love of the marvellous. Forged miracles, prophecies and supernatural events, which have been exposed in every age, show "the strong propensity of mankind to the extraordinary and the marvellous" and so should make us suspicious of such reports (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section X, Part II, §93, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)). Surprise and wonder are agreeable emotions, which gives a tendency to believe the events that produce them. Even people who cannot believe such events enjoy sharing the satisfaction "by rebound" and take pride in exciting others' admiration (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section X, Part II, §93, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)).

2. The pleasure of spreading news. Hume compares miracle reports to gossip about marriages in country towns. The pleasure of telling and being first to report spreads them, and he says the same passions, and stronger ones, incline people to report religious miracles with great vehemence (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section X, Part II, §93, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)).

3. Religion, enthusiasm, vanity and self-interest. When religion joins the love of wonder, common sense ends. A religionist may be an enthusiast who imagines what is not real, may knowingly persist in a falsehood for a holy cause, or may be moved by vanity and self-interest. His hearers often lack the judgement to examine his evidence, or have it disturbed by passion and a heated imagination. Their credulity increases his impudence, and his impudence overpowers their credulity (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section X, Part II, §93, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)).

4. Ignorant ancestors. Such stories abound chiefly among ignorant and barbarous nations. Civilized peoples are found to have received them from ignorant ancestors who passed them on with the authority that attends received opinions (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section X, Part II, §94, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). As we approach enlightened ages, prodigies thin out. Hume concludes that this reflects the usual human propensity to the marvellous, which learning may check at intervals but can never fully remove (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section X, Part II, §94, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)).

5. Humble beginnings of lies. Hume says that men have lied in all ages. The famous lies that grew to monstrous heights "arose from like beginnings" to those that were scorned and abandoned, but were "sown in a more proper soil" (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section X, Part II, §94, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)).

Hume therefore treats "the known and natural principles of credulity and delusion" as the obvious explanation. He notes that many such stories have been exposed early or have faded into oblivion. He asks whether we should prefer a miraculous violation of nature's laws to so natural a solution (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section X, Part II, §97, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
Hobbes treats a crime as a particular kind of sin. He defines a crime as "a sinne" that consists in committing, by deed or word, what the law forbids, or in omitting what it commands. From this he concludes that every crime is a sin, but not every sin is a crime (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 27, A Crime What, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)).

The main difference is whether another person can accuse you. Intending to steal or kill is a sin even if it never shows in word or act, because God sees thoughts and can charge them to a person. But until the intention appears through something done or said, it is not a crime, and "there is no place for humane accusation" of intentions that never appear outwardly (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 27, A Crime What, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)). Hobbes supports this with Greek and Latin vocabulary. The Greek word translated "sin" (amartema) covers any swerving from the law. The words translated "crime" cover only the sin of which one man may accuse another. Likewise the Latin peccatum covers every deviation from the law, while crimen covers only sins that can be made to appear before a judge, so it is not a mere intention (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 27, A Crime What, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)).

Sin is also the wider category in other respects. A sin is not only a transgression of a law but any contempt of the legislator, and it can lie in the intention or purpose to transgress (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 27, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)). Hobbes ties sin to law in general and crime to civil law specifically. Where law ceases, sin ceases, but the law of nature is eternal, so violations such as breaking covenants or ingratitude remain sins. When civil law ceases, crimes cease, because only the law of nature remains. Then each man is his own judge, accused only by his conscience. In that situation a wrongful act is a sin but not a crime (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 27, Where No Civill Law Is, There Is No Crime, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)).

He gives one further example of the line between the two. If a subject disobeys a command that conflicts with sovereignty, it is a sin. If he also resists a public minister in carrying it out, it becomes a crime (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 27, Excuses Against The Author, paragraph 29 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
Kant says that human reason cannot comprehend why the moral law is unconditionally necessary, but it can comprehend that this is beyond its grasp. The key statements are these:

1. Reason by its nature pushes its knowledge toward a consciousness of necessity. Yet it can discern the necessity of what is, happens, or ought to happen only by supposing a condition. Because it keeps seeking the unconditionally necessary, it is forced to assume it, "without any means of making it comprehensible to itself" (Immanuel Kant, Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals, Third Section, paragraph 35 (edition-specific)).

2. Kant treats this as a limit of human reason in general, not a flaw in his deduction of the supreme principle of morality. Reason cannot make us conceive the absolute necessity of an unconditional practical law such as the categorical imperative (Immanuel Kant, Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals, Third Section, paragraph 35 (edition-specific)). Reason cannot be blamed for refusing to explain this necessity by an assumed interest, because the law would then cease to be a supreme law of reason. So we do not comprehend the practical unconditional necessity of the moral imperative, but we do comprehend its incomprehensibility, which is all that can fairly be demanded of a philosophy that pushes its principles to the limit of human reason (Immanuel Kant, Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals, Third Section, paragraph 35 (edition-specific)).

3. Related limits appear elsewhere. Kant says it is impossible for us men to explain how and why the universality of the maxim as a law, that is, morality, interests us. He adds that this much is certain: the law does not bind us because it interests us, but interests us because it is valid for us (Immanuel Kant, Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals, Third Section, paragraph 31 (edition-specific)). Earlier, he notes that if the moral law were only presupposed in the idea of freedom, we could not prove its reality and objective necessity independently, and could give no satisfactory answer about why its validity must restrict our actions (Immanuel Kant, Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals, Third Section, paragraph 8 (edition-specific)). That passage is framed tentatively ("It seems then as if...").

4. These passages do not say the law's necessity is doubtful. In the Critique of Pure Reason, Kant says he assumes there are pure moral laws that are absolutely imperative and therefore in all respects necessary, and he considers himself warranted by enlightened moralists and by every person's moral judgement (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Doctrine of Method, Chapter 2, Section II, paragraph 8 (edition-specific)). The supplied passages do not go further than this to explain how reason relates to that necessity.

top_retrieved.author: John Locke
top_retrieved.work: An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1 / MDCXC, Based on the 2nd Edition, Books 1 and 2

detail.answer:
Locke says the bond sometimes lasts beyond mating because the purpose of the male–female union is not just procreation but "the continuation of the species." So the union should last after procreation for as long as the young need nourishment and support, until they can provide for themselves (Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 7, §79, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)). He treats this as a rule set by the Creator that the "inferior creatures" steadily obey (same passage).

He illustrates this with different animals. Among grass-feeding viviparous animals (those bearing live young), the bond ends with copulation. The mother's teat is enough to nourish the young until they can feed on grass, so the male can contribute nothing to their sustenance (Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 7, §79, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)). Among beasts of prey the bond lasts longer. The mother cannot easily support herself and her numerous offspring by her own prey alone, so the male's help is needed for the family until the young can prey for themselves (same passage). Birds are similar. Their young need food in the nest, so the cock and hen stay mates until the young can use their wings and provide for themselves. Locke notes exceptions among some domestic birds, where plentiful food excuses the cock from feeding the brood (same passage).

For humans, Locke offers a further reason, which he states tentatively as "the chief, if not the only reason." The female can conceive again and commonly bears a new child before the previous one is independent, so the father is obliged to stay with the same woman longer. In other creatures the young can subsist before procreation returns, so the conjugal bond dissolves of itself (Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 7, §80, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
Smith points to several weaknesses, in two settings. Both come from the passages on forts and garrisons.

1. The committee that maintains forts and garrisons, funded by a parliamentary grant of about £13,000 a year (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book V, Chapter 1, Part III, paragraph 37 (edition-specific)).
- Oversight is weak. The committee must account annually to the cursitor baron of exchequer, and the account is then laid before parliament. Smith says parliament gives so little attention to millions that it is unlikely to give much to £13,000 a year. He adds that the cursitor baron, given his profession and education, is unlikely to be profoundly skilled in the proper expense of forts and garrisons. (same passage)
- Naval captains or other officers appointed by the board of admiralty may inquire into the forts and garrisons and report to that board. But the board seems to have no direct jurisdiction over the committee and no authority to correct those it inquires into. The captains are also not supposed to be deeply learned in fortification. (same passage)
- Sanctions are weak. The utmost punishment seems to be removal from an office held for only three years and with very small lawful emoluments, unless there is direct malversation or embezzlement. Smith says the fear of this can never be a strong enough motive to force continual, careful attention to a business in which the committee-man has no other interest. (same passage)
- Smith also reports that the committee was accused of sending bricks and stones from England to repair Cape Coast Castle, for which parliament had several times granted extra money. The passage as given breaks off after saying these were said to be of bad quality, so it does not show the rest of his account. (same passage)

2. Regulated companies as keepers of forts and garrisons (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book V, Chapter 1, Part III, paragraph 34 (edition-specific)).
- Smith says regulated companies seem much more unfit for this service than joint-stock companies. (same passage)
- Their directors have no particular interest in the prosperity of the company's general trade, for whose sake the forts and garrisons are maintained. Decay of that trade may even benefit their own private trade. (same passage)
- They manage no common capital. They have only the casual revenue from admission fines and corporation duties, so even with the same interest they can seldom have the same ability to make their attention effectual. (same passage; Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book V, Chapter 1, Part III, paragraph 34 (edition-specific))

The passages do not say how these problems should be fixed beyond the comparison with joint-stock companies.

detail.question: What does Hume say about the certainty of the science that studies the mind?
detail.answer:
Hume defends the certainty of the science of the mind, though he admits it is difficult. In Section I he says there should be no suspicion that this science is "uncertain and chimerical" (fanciful or unreal), unless one adopts a scepticism that would undermine all speculation and even action (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section I, §8, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)). His reasons are that the mind has distinct powers and faculties, that what is distinct in immediate perception can be distinguished by reflexion, and so there is a truth and falsehood about these matters that lies within human understanding (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section I, §8, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)). Obvious distinctions, such as will versus understanding or imagination versus passions, are grasped by everyone. The finer, more philosophical distinctions are "no less real and certain, though more difficult to be comprehended" (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section I, §8, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)). He also points to recent successes as grounds for a juster notion of the certainty and solidity of this branch of learning (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section I, §8, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)).

He qualifies this by stressing difficulty. Mental operations, though intimately present to us, seem obscure when reflected upon, and their boundaries are hard to find. So merely distinguishing and classing them is a real achievement, a "mental geography" (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section I, §8, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). He adds that the chief obstacle in the moral or metaphysical sciences is the obscurity of ideas and ambiguity of terms. He also says that, in tracing the principles of the human mind, nature soon bars further enquiry into causes, so we may be satisfied with progress through a few steps (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section VII, Part I, §48, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)). The mind's command over itself is likewise limited, and those limits are known only by experience, not by reason (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section VII, Part I, §53, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)).

The passages do not give a fuller account of how certain this science is compared with others beyond these points.

detail.answer:
Burke raises several concerns about how the confiscated Church lands are being managed financially.

1. **The fund was supposed to be free of charges, but new ones keep being added.** The Assembly pledged that Church estates would be "disengaged of all charges" once the costs of religion, the poor and ecclesiastical pensions were provided for (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 403 (edition-specific)). Burke says they then loaded the fund with new charges. These include compensation for the disbanded judiciary and suppressed offices, which he says "unquestionably amounts to many French millions." They also include an annuity of £480,000 sterling for the interest on the first assignats (the paper currency issued against the lands) (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 406 (edition-specific)).

2. **The costs of management have not been fairly stated.** Burke asks whether the Assembly has ever honestly stated the expense of managing the lands. They are in the hands of municipalities and a "legion of unknown under-agents" (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 406 (edition-specific)). He also says an open and exact statement of the property's value, and of the time, circumstances and place of sale, was needed to remove the stigma attached to land-banks. It was also needed to keep faith with the Assembly's earlier pledge (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 403 (edition-specific)).

3. **A sudden sale would have defeated the profits.** Putting this huge mass of land on the market at once would depreciate the lands, and indeed all French landed estates. It would also divert circulating money from trade to land (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 219 (edition-specific)).

4. **The sale terms favor purchasers without money.** Only a portion of the price is paid up front, with twelve years allowed for the rest. Burke argues this lets in "a body of purchasers without money," making the sale a sort of gift. The purchasers would pay from rents, from stripping buildings and woods, and from squeezing the peasants, rather than the state receiving the rents (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 222 (edition-specific)).

5. **The scheme undermines public credit.** Burke says only desperate adventurers would destroy the settled revenue of the state, "the sole security for the public credit," in the hope of rebuilding it from confiscated property. He holds that the authors of the scheme were bound to make their bank a real fund of credit, as far as such a bank could be (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 401 (edition-specific)).

The passages do not give full figures for the management costs. Burke himself says he cannot ascertain the total of the new charges (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 406 (edition-specific)).

detail.question: What misconception about the meaning of 'utility' does Mill address in this paragraph?
detail.answer: In this paragraph Mill addresses the "ignorant blunder" of supposing that those who uphold utility as the test of right and wrong use "utility" in a narrow, colloquial sense in which it is opposed to pleasure (Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 2, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). He says the opposite accusation, that utilitarianism refers everything to pleasure in its grossest form, is also commonly made, often by the very same people (Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 2, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). In fact, he says, every writer from Epicurus to Bentham who maintained the theory meant by utility not something distinct from pleasure but "pleasure itself, together with exemption from pain". They declared that the useful includes the agreeable and the ornamental, among other things (Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 2, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). The popular misuse is that people who know only the sound of the word "utilitarian" take it to mean the rejection or neglect of pleasure in some forms, such as beauty, ornament or amusement. Occasionally it is used as a compliment, implying superiority to frivolity (Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 2, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). Mill adds that this perverted use is the only one in which the word is popularly known, and the source of the new generation's sole notion of its meaning. He says those who introduced the word may feel called upon to resume it to rescue it from this degradation (Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 2, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
Burke objects to the constant talk of resistance and revolution for several connected reasons, all drawn from the passages on the anniversary sermons.

1. It makes an extreme remedy into a daily habit. He says he never liked "this continual talk of resistance and revolution, or the practice of making the extreme medicine of the Constitution its daily bread." He argues that this makes society dangerously "valetudinary" (sickly, prone to invalidism), comparing it to taking regular doses of poison and provocatives to our love of liberty (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 112 (edition-specific)). He also warns that such sermons may cheat people of the principles and benefits of the very Revolution they commemorate (same passage).

2. It wears out the spirit needed for real emergencies. This "distemper of remedy, grown habitual" wears out, by vulgar and prostituted use, the spring of spirit that should be saved for great occasions. He points to Roman boys practicing themes of tyrannicide in a servile period (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 113 (edition-specific)). He says that in ordinary times it produces the worst effects even on the cause of liberty (same passage).

3. It produces unreliable, impractical politicians. Burke says that many high-bred republicans soon became thorough-paced courtiers. Finding their extreme principles unfit for cases that need only a qualified, civil and legal resistance, they employ no resistance at all, since for them it is "a war or a revolution, or it is nothing." They come to think lightly of all public principle. Hypocrisy, he adds, delights in sublime speculation because it never intends to go beyond it (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 113 (edition-specific)).

4. It makes constant projectors of change bad citizens. Those who keep some change in Church or State always in view regard the actual state as of no estimation. They rejoice in bad public management as more propitious to revolution, and they judge people and principles only by whether they advance their design of change. They swing between the most stretched prerogative and the wildest democratic ideas without regard to cause, person or party (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 113 (edition-specific)).

5. It lets the spirit of liberty evaporate. Burke calls such talk "flippant, vain discourse" in which people let the spirit of liberty evaporate, and he thinks it worth observing mainly because it supports the scheme of "cashiering kings for misconduct" (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 52 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
The passages give two main points about gallantry, though they do not offer a full treatment.

**Effects on women.** Wollstonecraft says the "cold unmeaning intercourse of gallantry" has rendered many women "vain and useless," and she compares this with the unhappiness love has caused some (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 5, §3, paragraph 6 (edition-specific)). She calls this "heartless attention to the sex" a vestige of "gothic manners" (relics of medieval custom). It is reckoned manly and polite, so she fears it will not disappear until society is organized very differently (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 5, §3, paragraph 6 (edition-specific)).

**Effects on society.** She says gallantry has a "imaginary dignity" and is a mere "lip-service" that prevails in the most civilized European states alongside "extreme dissoluteness of morals." Using Portugal as her example, she says it takes the place of serious moral obligations. A man is seldom assassinated in a woman's company, yet the lady is asked to pardon the rudeness and depart, even if sprinkled with her husband's or brother's blood (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 5, §3, paragraph 6 (edition-specific)).

Elsewhere she calls the "impudent dross of gallantry, thought so manly" disgusting. She asks whether the insulting stare it licenses is really "respect for the sex." She argues that it reveals "habitual depravity" and "weakness of mind," so it is vain to expect much public or private virtue until men and women grow more modest. She contrasts gallantry with true respect, the "modest respect of humanity, and fellow-feeling," and calls gallantry a "libidinous mockery" and, alongside it, the "insolent condescension of protectorship" (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 7, paragraph 13 (edition-specific)).

**Limits of the passages.** The other passages supplied discuss women's duties and civil existence, but they do not mention gallantry directly, so I do not attribute further claims about it to her.

detail.answer:
Burke argues that the new French Constitution cuts the link between the people and their representatives, and he contrasts it with the British Constitution.

**No real connection between the people and the deputy.** He says there is "little, or rather no, connection between the last representative and the first constituent." The member who goes to the National Assembly is not chosen by the people or accountable to them, because three elections and two sets of magistracy come between him and the primary assembly. This makes him "an ambassador of a state, and not the representative of the people within a state." (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 326 (edition-specific))

**No fix is possible without undoing the scheme.** Burke says that restoring the link would mean the primary electors forcing the later electors to choose as they wish. That would bring back the "tumult and confusion of popular election" the graded elections were meant to avoid. Unless the people break up this gradation, he says, they do not substantially elect to the Assembly at all. (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 326 (edition-specific))

**The Assembly as a congress of ambassadors.** Burke describes the scheme as tending to split France into independent republics. Their only connection would be acquiescence in the decisions of a general congress of ambassadors from each republic, which he says is what the National Assembly is. (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 318 (edition-specific))

**Contrast with Britain.** In France the elective Assembly is "the sovereign, and the sole sovereign," so its members are integral parts of that sovereignty. In Britain, he says, the representative separated from the other parts "can have no action and no existence." The government is the point of reference for the members, and it is a trustee for the whole rather than for the parts. The King and the Lords are securities for the equality of each district. (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 325 (edition-specific)) He adds that Britain's representation has been found "perfectly adequate to all the purposes for which a representation of the people can be desired or devised." (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 98 (edition-specific))

**Missing intermediate body.** Burke also faults the French for providing no senate or similar council. He says such a body holds a middle place between the supreme power exercised by the people, or delegated from them, and the mere executive. (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 345 (edition-specific))

**Predicted result.** If the Constitution continues, he believes France will be governed by an "ignoble oligarchy" of local agitators, speculators and similar figures, which would end the dreams of equality. This is stated as his belief. (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 339 (edition-specific))
